Diabetes.description: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic condition characterized by elevated levels of blood glucose over a prolonged period due to insufficient insulin production or ineffective insulin utilization.
symptoms: Frequent urination (polyuria)
Excessive thirst (polydipsia)
Unexplained weight loss
Increased hunger
Fatigue and weakness
Blurred vision
Slow-healing cuts or sores
risk_factors: Physical inactivity and sedentary lifestyle
Family history of diabetes
Overweight or obesity
High blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol levels
Age (45 years or older for Type 2)

prefer: Non-starchy vegetables (spinach, broccoli, peppers)
Whole grains (brown rice, oats, quinoa)
Legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas)
Lean proteins (poultry, tofu, fish)
Healthy fats (nuts, seeds, olive oil)
limit: Sugar-sweetened beverages and sodas
Refined carbohydrates and white bread
Ultra-processed snack foods and pastries
High saturated and trans fat foods
food.general_tip: Focus on consistent carbohydrate intake, high-fiber foods, and balanced portion sizes throughout the day.

recommended: Brisk walking (at least 150 minutes per week)
Cycling or stationary biking
Swimming or water aerobics
Moderate resistance and strength training (2-3 days per week)
Gentle stretching and yoga
precautions: Monitor blood sugar levels before and after intense physical activity if advised by a doctor.
Stay well hydrated and carry a fast-acting glucose source if prone to low blood sugar.
Wear supportive footwear to prevent foot injuries and inspect feet regularly.

lifestyle: Maintain consistent sleep schedule (7-8 hours per night)
Avoid smoking and tobacco products
Manage psychological stress through relaxation techniques
Maintain a healthy body weight
monitoring: Regular self-monitoring of blood glucose levels as recommended by a doctor
Periodic HbA1c testing (typically every 3 to 6 months)
Annual dilated eye examinations and comprehensive foot exams
Routine kidney function (eGFR, microalbumin) and lipid profile checks
medical_guidance: Work closely with an endocrinologist, certified diabetes educator, or primary care provider.
Attend regular diabetes self-management education sessions.
Never adjust prescribed insulin or medications without direct clinician consultation.
warning_signs: Extreme dizziness, confusion, or shakiness (severe hypoglycemia)
Fruity-smelling breath, nausea, vomiting, or rapid breathing (possible diabetic ketoacidosis)
Sudden vision loss or dark floating spots
Non-healing ulcers or loss of sensation in the feet
when_to_seek_help: Blood glucose readings are persistently very high or dangerously low
Signs of severe dehydration, vomiting, or confusion occur
Presence of foot redness, warmth, or open sores that do not heal
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Diabetes Fact Sheet
American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Medical Care
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Diabetes

Heart Disease.description: Heart disease refers to several types of heart conditions, most commonly coronary artery disease, which affects blood flow to the heart and can lead to heart attacks or other complications.
symptoms: Chest discomfort, pressure, or fullness (angina)
Shortness of breath during exertion or rest
Pain or discomfort in the neck, jaw, throat, back, or arms
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting
Unexplained fatigue and coldness in extremities
risk_factors: High blood pressure (hypertension)
Elevated LDL cholesterol and triglycerides
Tobacco use and smoking
Diabetes and insulin resistance
Family history of early cardiovascular disease

prefer: Fresh fruits and leafy green vegetables
Fatty fish rich in Omega-3 (salmon, mackerel, sardines)
Whole grain cereals, oats, and brown rice
Nuts (walnuts, almonds) and seeds
Monounsaturated fats like extra virgin olive oil
limit: High-sodium foods, canned soups, and salty snacks
Processed meats (bacon, sausages, hot dogs)
Fried and commercially baked goods with trans fats
Excessive alcohol consumption
food.general_tip: Follow a heart-healthy dietary pattern (such as Mediterranean or DASH style) low in sodium and saturated fat.

recommended: Moderate-intensity walking
Low-impact cycling or stationary riding
Supervised cardiac rehabilitation exercise programs if prescribed
Light resistance band training
precautions: Always warm up and cool down gradually.
Stop immediately if you feel chest pain, severe dizziness, or palpitations.
Consult a cardiologist before starting any new or vigorous exercise routine.

lifestyle: Completely quit smoking and avoid secondhand smoke
Practice daily stress reduction and deep breathing exercises
Maintain a healthy waist circumference and body mass index
Limit caffeine and stimulant intake if experiencing palpitations
monitoring: Regular home and clinical blood pressure monitoring
Periodic lipid panel tests (cholesterol and triglycerides)
Periodic electrocardiograms (ECG) and echocardiograms as advised
Tracking resting heart rate and daily symptoms
medical_guidance: Maintain regular appointments with a qualified cardiologist or physician.
Take all prescribed cardiovascular therapies strictly as directed.
Understand your target numbers for blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, and blood sugar.
warning_signs: Crushing chest pain radiating to the left arm, jaw, or back
Sudden, unexplained shortness of breath with cold sweats
Loss of consciousness or severe sudden dizziness
Rapid or irregular heartbeat accompanied by weakness
when_to_seek_help: Any sudden or worsening chest pain or tightness occurs (call emergency services immediately)
Increasing shortness of breath while lying flat or during light tasks
Sudden unexplained swelling in legs, ankles, or feet
sources: National Health Service (NHS) - Coronary Heart Disease

dataset_info.dataset_name: Heart Disease (Cleveland/Hungarian), Heart Failure Clinical Records, Statlog Heart

Heart Failure.description: Heart failure is a progressive condition where the heart muscle is unable to pump blood efficiently enough to meet the body's normal needs for blood and oxygen.
common_types: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)
symptoms: Shortness of breath (dyspnea) during activity or when lying flat
Persistent coughing or wheezing with white or pink blood-tinged phlegm
Swelling (edema) in feet, ankles, legs, or abdomen
Rapid or irregular heartbeat
Sudden unexplained weight gain from fluid retention
Persistent fatigue and weakness
risk_factors: Coronary artery disease and past heart attack
Chronic high blood pressure
Diabetes and metabolic syndrome
Valvular heart disease or congenital defects
Severe sleep apnea

prefer: Fresh vegetables and fruits naturally low in sodium
Skinless poultry, beans, and lentils
Whole grain bread and cereals
Herbs and spices for seasoning instead of table salt
limit: Excess sodium (typically keep below 1,500 - 2,000 mg/day as advised by doctor)
Processed foods, deli meats, and frozen dinners
Excessive fluid intake if fluid restriction has been ordered
Alcohol and caffeinated energy drinks
food.general_tip: Strictly monitor daily sodium and fluid intake to prevent fluid retention.

recommended: Gradual, low-intensity walking on flat surfaces
Seated stretching and mobility exercises
Structured cardiac rehabilitation program under medical supervision
precautions: Avoid heavy weightlifting or isometric straining.
Do not exercise if you feel breathless, dizzy, or notice sudden swelling.
Always rest whenever fatigue sets in.

lifestyle: Daily morning weight recording after urinating and before eating
Elevate legs when resting to reduce lower limb swelling
Get vaccinated against influenza and pneumococcal disease
Strictly avoid smoking and alcohol
monitoring: Daily body weight log (report gains of >2-3 lbs in a day or >5 lbs in a week)
Blood pressure and resting pulse monitoring
Routine kidney function (creatinine, BUN) and electrolyte blood tests
Periodic echocardiograms to evaluate ejection fraction
medical_guidance: Follow an individualized heart failure action plan developed with your cardiology team.
Take all medications regularly and never skip doses.
Know your target weight and notify your doctor when weight fluctuates rapidly.
warning_signs: Severe shortness of breath that prevents talking or sleeping
Coughing up pink, foamy mucus
Rapid weight gain of more than 3 pounds in 24 hours
New or worsening confusion, dizziness, or fainting
when_to_seek_help: Sudden worsening of breathing difficulty or chest pain
Marked swelling spreading rapidly to knees, thighs, or abdomen
Frequent episodes of lightheadedness upon standing
sources: American College of Cardiology (ACC) / AHA Heart Failure Guidelines

Stroke.description: A stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted or reduced, preventing brain tissue from getting oxygen and nutrients, which can cause brain cells to begin dying within minutes.
common_types: Hemorrhagic Stroke (ruptured blood vessel in brain)
symptoms: Sudden numbness or weakness of the face, arm, or leg (especially on one side)
Sudden confusion, trouble speaking, or difficulty understanding speech
Sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes
Sudden trouble walking, loss of balance, dizziness, or lack of coordination
Sudden severe headache with no known cause
risk_factors: High blood pressure (hypertension)
Smoking and tobacco use
Atrial fibrillation or heart conditions
Diabetes and high cholesterol
Previous stroke or Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)

prefer: Vegetables, leafy greens, and colorful fruits
Fish, legumes, and lean poultry
Whole grain bread, oats, and barley
Healthy cooking oils like olive oil
limit: Salty and sodium-rich preserved foods
High saturated fat foods and deep-fried dishes
Processed meats and sugary snacks
Heavy alcohol intake
food.general_tip: Adopt a low-sodium, potassium-rich, antioxidant-dense diet to protect vascular health.

recommended: Post-stroke physical therapy and rehabilitation exercises
Gentle daily walking with supportive assistance if needed
Balance, coordination, and range-of-motion routines
Stationary recumbent cycling
precautions: Exercise only under guidance of a physical or occupational therapist if mobility is impaired.
Use assistive devices (canes, walkers) to prevent falls.
Avoid sudden, high-intensity exertion that spikes blood pressure.

lifestyle: Keep blood pressure in the recommended target range
Manage sleep apnea if diagnosed
Maintain cognitive stimulation through puzzles and reading
Avoid all tobacco products
monitoring: Frequent blood pressure checks
Periodic carotid ultrasound or neuroimaging follow-ups as advised
Blood glucose and lipid profile surveillance
Monitoring for heart rhythm irregularities (such as atrial fibrillation)
medical_guidance: Remember the F.A.S.T. signs: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency.
Attend regular neurological follow-ups and complete prescribed rehabilitation therapies.
Take prescribed antiplatelet, anticoagulant, or blood pressure therapies faithfully.
warning_signs: Sudden facial asymmetry or drooping corner of mouth
Inability to lift or hold up one arm
Slurred speech, garbled words, or inability to speak
Sudden vision blackout or double vision
when_to_seek_help: ANY sudden sign of stroke (FAST) requires IMMEDIATE emergency response (call 911 / 112 / local emergency).
Even if symptoms resolve after a few minutes (suspected TIA), immediate emergency evaluation is essential.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Stroke

Alzheimers_Disease.description: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that slowly destroys memory, thinking skills, and eventually the ability to carry out simple daily tasks.
symptoms: Memory loss that disrupts daily life
Challenges in planning or solving problems
Difficulty completing familiar tasks
Confusion with time or place
Trouble understanding visual images and spatial relationships
New problems with words in speaking or writing
Changes in mood, personality, and social withdrawal
risk_factors: Advancing age (65 years and older)
Family history and genetics (APOE-e4 allele)
Cardiovascular risk factors (high BP, diabetes, high cholesterol)
History of severe head trauma or brain injury
Chronic lack of mental and social engagement

prefer: MIND / Mediterranean diet foods (leafy greens, berries, olive oil)
Fatty fish (salmon, tuna) containing DHA and EPA
Nuts, seeds, and legumes
Whole grains and colorful vegetables
limit: Saturated fats, butter, and stick margarine
Pastries, sweets, and refined sugars
High-sodium processed meats
Heavy alcohol consumption
food.general_tip: Follow a MIND or Mediterranean-style dietary pattern rich in brain-protective antioxidants and omega-3 fatty acids.

recommended: Daily supervised walking in safe, familiar environments
Simple chair yoga, balance, and stretching exercises
Light aerobic activities and gentle dancing
Gardening and household movement
precautions: Provide supervision to prevent wandering and fall injuries.
Ensure clutter-free walking paths with adequate lighting.
Keep physical routines simple, calm, and familiar.

lifestyle: Establish consistent, predictable daily routines
Engage in mentally stimulating activities (reading, music, simple games)
Maintain active social interactions with family and friends
Ensure home safety (remove trip hazards, install handrails)
monitoring: Periodic cognitive assessments (such as MMSE, MoCA) by a neurologist
Monitoring behavioral changes, sleep patterns, and appetite
Regular medication safety reviews and fall risk evaluations
medical_guidance: Work in close partnership with a neurologist, geriatrician, and memory care team.
Engage caregiver support resources and community support groups.
Plan legal, financial, and healthcare advance directives early.
warning_signs: Getting lost in familiar neighborhood environments
Inability to recognize close family members
Severe agitation, paranoia, hallucinations, or aggression
Difficulty swallowing, choking, or extreme weight loss
when_to_seek_help: Sudden, acute worsening of confusion or delirium (may indicate infection like UTI)
Frequent falls or unsteadiness
Severe sleep disturbances or wandering behaviors
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Dementia Fact Sheet

Parkinsons_Disease.description: Parkinson's disease is a progressive movement disorder of the central nervous system caused by the degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain.
symptoms: Tremor at rest (especially in hands, arms, legs, or jaw)
Slowness of movement (bradykinesia)
Muscle stiffness and rigidity
Impaired balance, posture, and coordination
Softened speech (hypophonia) and smaller handwriting (micrographia)
Sleep disturbances, loss of smell, and constipation
risk_factors: Age (typically develops around age 60 or older)
Genetic predisposition and specific gene mutations
Male gender (slightly higher incidence)
Prolonged exposure to certain pesticides and industrial toxins

prefer: High-fiber foods (beans, oats, prunes, vegetables) to prevent constipation
Hydrating fluids and water throughout the day
Antioxidant-rich foods (berries, spinach, green tea)
Small, balanced, easy-to-chew meals
limit: Heavy protein meals taken at the exact same time as levodopa medication (as protein can compete with absorption)
High-fat, hard-to-digest processed foods
Excessive intake of refined sugars and caffeine
food.general_tip: Maintain high fiber and adequate hydration; discuss timing of dietary protein relative to medication schedule with your doctor.

recommended: Targeted physical therapy and gait training
Tai Chi and yoga for balance and flexibility
Tandem cycling or stationary cycling
Speech and voice exercises (e.g., LSVT LOUD)
precautions: Take precautions to prevent falls; use walking poles or handrails if balance is compromised.
Avoid exercising during 'off' medication periods when stiffness is highest.
Perform movements on non-slip surfaces.

lifestyle: Modify home environment for fall prevention (remove rugs, install grab bars)
Wear non-skid, supportive shoes without rubber grips that catch on carpets
Prioritize restful sleep hygiene and manage daytime fatigue
Practice daily vocal and facial muscle exercises
monitoring: Regular neurological evaluations using movement rating scales (UPDRS)
Tracking motor fluctuations ('on' vs 'off' medication times)
Monitoring blood pressure when standing (to detect orthostatic hypotension)
Swallowing and speech assessments by speech-language therapists
medical_guidance: Consult a movement disorder specialist or neurologist regularly.
Take Parkinson's medications strictly on time according to the prescribed schedule.
Include physical, occupational, and speech therapists in ongoing care.
warning_signs: Sudden freezing of gait leading to falls
Severe difficulty swallowing or recurrent coughing while eating
Visual hallucinations or sudden confusion
Severe drop in blood pressure with dizziness when standing up
when_to_seek_help: Frequent falls or inability to walk safely
Signs of aspiration or severe choking episodes
Sudden emergence of hallucinations or medication side effects
sources: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS)

Epilepsy.description: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by sudden surges of abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
symptoms: Temporary confusion or staring spells
Uncontrollable jerking movements of arms and legs
Loss of consciousness or awareness
Unusual sensations, emotions, or smells (auras)
Stiffening of muscles followed by rhythmic twitching
risk_factors: Past head trauma or brain injury
Stroke or vascular brain conditions
Brain infections (meningitis, encephalitis)
Genetic predisposition
Complications during fetal development or birth

prefer: Balanced meals with steady nutrient release
Magnesium-rich foods (leafy greens, pumpkin seeds, whole grains)
Adequate water and electrolyte hydration
Medically supervised ketogenic/modified Atkins diet if specifically prescribed for refractory epilepsy
limit: Excessive caffeine and energy drinks
Alcohol and recreational substances
Skipping meals or extreme fasting (which can trigger seizures)
food.general_tip: Maintain regular, balanced meals and consistent hydration to prevent metabolic triggers.

recommended: Regular moderate aerobic exercise (walking, jogging)
Strength training with machines rather than free heavy weights
Pilates and yoga for stress reduction
precautions: Never swim alone; always have a companion who knows seizure first-aid.
Avoid unsupervised high-altitude climbing or solo water sports.
Wear protective headgear during cycling or contact sports.

lifestyle: Ensure consistent, adequate sleep (sleep deprivation is a major seizure trigger)
Avoid known individual seizure triggers (e.g., flashing lights, extreme fatigue)
Wear medical alert identification detailing the epilepsy diagnosis
Manage emotional stress through mindfulness and relaxation
monitoring: Maintain a detailed seizure diary (date, time, duration, triggers, symptoms)
Periodic electroencephalogram (EEG) and brain MRI evaluations
Routine therapeutic drug monitoring for antiepileptic medication levels
medical_guidance: Consult an epileptologist or neurologist regularly.
Take antiepileptic medications strictly as prescribed without missing doses.
Ensure family, friends, and coworkers know basic seizure first aid (turn person to side, do not put anything in mouth).
warning_signs: Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes (status epilepticus)
Repeated seizures occurring without regaining consciousness between them
Difficulty breathing or remaining unconscious after seizure ends
Seizure occurring in water or resulting in serious injury
when_to_seek_help: Call emergency services immediately if a seizure lasts >5 minutes, repeats rapidly, or happens for the first time.
Seek medical review if seizure frequency increases or new seizure types appear.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Epilepsy Fact Sheet
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Epilepsy

Brain_Tumor.description: A brain tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of cells in the brain or surrounding tissues, which can be benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous).
symptoms: New onset or change in pattern of severe headaches (often worse in the morning)
Unexplained nausea or vomiting
Vision problems (blurred vision, double vision, loss of peripheral vision)
Gradual loss of sensation or movement in an arm or leg
Difficulty with balance and coordination
Speech difficulties and personality/behavioral changes
New onset seizures
risk_factors: Exposure to ionizing radiation
Family history of rare genetic syndromes (e.g., Neurofibromatosis, Li-Fraumeni)
Advanced age (risk varies by specific tumor type)

prefer: Nutrient-dense, antioxidant-rich fruits and vegetables
Adequate lean protein (poultry, eggs, legumes, fish) to support recovery
Small, frequent meals if nausea is present
Plenty of fluids to stay well hydrated
limit: Excessive refined sugars and highly processed foods
Heavy, greasy, or spicy foods that aggravate nausea
Alcohol and tobacco
food.general_tip: Focus on high-protein, calorie-sufficient, easy-to-digest meals to support neurological health and treatment recovery.

recommended: Gentle walking and light stretching as tolerated
Physical and occupational therapy rehabilitation
Seated mobility exercises
precautions: Avoid activities with fall risks if balance or vision is impaired.
Do not perform heavy straining or inverted poses that increase intracranial pressure.
Rest whenever fatigued; avoid pushing through exhaustion.

lifestyle: Ensure a quiet, restful sleeping environment
Use assistive devices and remove household fall hazards
Seek emotional and psychological counseling support
Keep a symptom log to share with the neuro-oncology team
monitoring: Serial brain MRI or CT imaging to monitor tumor dimensions
Regular neurological examinations, visual field testing, and cognitive assessments
Monitoring for seizures and medication side effects
medical_guidance: Work with a multidisciplinary team (neurosurgeon, neuro-oncologist, radiation oncologist).
Follow surgical, radiation, or chemotherapy treatment plans closely.
Report any new or worsening neurological deficits promptly.
warning_signs: Sudden, excruciating headache unlike any previous headache
Sudden loss of consciousness or onset of seizures
Rapid weakness, paralysis, or inability to speak
Persistent, projectile vomiting
when_to_seek_help: Immediate emergency care for new seizures, sudden paralysis, or loss of responsiveness.
Prompt medical evaluation for persistent, unexplained morning headaches with nausea.

Multiple_Sclerosis.description: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system in which the immune system attacks the protective myelin sheath covering nerve fibers.
symptoms: Numbness, tingling, or weakness in one or more limbs
Vision loss, double vision, or pain during eye movement (optic neuritis)
Electric-shock sensations occurring with certain neck movements (Lhermitte sign)
Severe fatigue and brain fog
Unsteady gait, lack of coordination, or tremors
Bladder and bowel dysfunction
risk_factors: Age (typically diagnosed between 20 and 40 years)
Female gender (more common in women)
Low Vitamin D levels and low sunlight exposure
Smoking
Family history of MS
Past Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection

prefer: Anti-inflammatory foods (fatty fish, walnuts, flaxseeds)
Vitamin D-rich foods (fortified dairy/plant milk, egg yolks, mushrooms)
High-fiber vegetables and whole grains to support gut health
Adequate water intake
limit: Saturated fats and trans fats
Ultra-processed packaged foods
Excess sodium and refined sugars
food.general_tip: Emphasize an anti-inflammatory, nutrient-dense diet rich in Vitamin D and Omega-3 fatty acids.

recommended: Water aerobics and swimming (cool water prevents heat-induced fatigue)
Stationary cycling and elliptical training
Stretching, Pilates, and adapted yoga for spasticity
Supervised physical therapy
precautions: Avoid overheating (Uhthoff phenomenon can temporarily worsen symptoms).
Use cooling vests, fans, and cold drinks during workouts.
Rest frequently and avoid exercising to the point of exhaustion.

lifestyle: Avoid heat exposure (hot tubs, saunas, direct midday sun)
Strictly quit smoking (smoking accelerates MS progression)
Prioritize energy conservation techniques and daytime pacing
Engage in stress management and mindfulness
monitoring: Periodic brain and spinal cord MRI scans to evaluate lesion activity
Routine neurological functional assessments (EDSS)
Monitoring Vitamin D blood levels
Tracking flare-ups, relapses, and recovery patterns
medical_guidance: Collaborate regularly with an MS specialist neurologist.
Discuss disease-modifying therapies (DMTs) to reduce relapse frequency and slow progression.
Never discontinue DMTs without consulting your healthcare provider.
warning_signs: Sudden new neurological deficit or severe relapse lasting >24 hours
Rapid loss of vision in one eye
Severe loss of bladder or bowel control
Signs of severe infection or fever during immunosuppressive therapy
when_to_seek_help: Contact your MS care team promptly upon onset of a new relapse or acute symptom worsening.
Seek urgent medical evaluation for sudden vision impairment or acute severe weakness.

Anemia.description: Anemia is a condition in which the blood has a lower than normal number of healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin, leading to reduced oxygen flow to the body's organs.
symptoms: Persistent fatigue, weakness, and low energy
Pale, yellowish skin and pale inner eyelids
Shortness of breath and dizziness, especially on standing
Cold hands and feet
Headaches and lightheadedness
Brittle nails or unusual cravings for non-food items like ice (pica)
risk_factors: Diet low in iron, vitamin B12, or folate
Heavy menstrual bleeding
Pregnancy
Chronic blood loss (e.g., gastrointestinal ulcers, polyps)
Intestinal absorption disorders (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn's)

prefer: Iron-rich foods (spinach, lentils, beans, fortified cereals, lean red meat)
Vitamin C foods (oranges, bell peppers, tomatoes) to enhance iron absorption
Vitamin B12 sources (eggs, dairy, fish, fortified nutritional yeast)
Folate-rich leafy greens, asparagus, and citrus fruits
limit: Drinking tea or coffee directly with iron-rich meals (tannins inhibit absorption)
Excessive calcium supplements taken at the exact same time as iron foods
Excessive alcohol intake
food.general_tip: Combine plant-based iron sources with Vitamin C-rich foods to maximize dietary iron absorption.

recommended: Low-intensity walking and gentle mobility exercises
Light stretching and breathing routines
Gradual progression of activity as hemoglobin levels improve
precautions: Avoid high-intensity or strenuous workouts until hemoglobin levels stabilize.
Rest immediately if feeling dizzy, lightheaded, or short of breath.
Change positions slowly to avoid postural dizziness.

lifestyle: Prioritize restful sleep and plan rest breaks during the day
Avoid intense overexertion
Maintain routine health checks to identify underlying causes of blood loss
monitoring: Periodic Complete Blood Count (CBC) and hemoglobin checks
Serum ferritin, iron saturation, and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC)
Vitamin B12 and serum folate levels
medical_guidance: Always investigate the underlying root cause of anemia with a physician.
Take iron or vitamin supplements only in the dosage recommended by your clinician.
Avoid self-treating severe fatigue without proper lab confirmation.
warning_signs: Severe shortness of breath at rest
Chest pain or rapid, pounding heartbeat (palpitations)
Fainting spells (syncope) or extreme pallor
Black, tarry stools or visible blood in vomit or stool
when_to_seek_help: Immediate emergency evaluation for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or black tarry stools.
Schedule a doctor visit if persistent fatigue and pale skin do not improve.
sources: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI / NIH)
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Iron and Iron Deficiency

Leukemia.description: Leukemia is a cancer of the blood-forming tissues, including bone marrow and lymphatic system, which results in the rapid overproduction of abnormal, non-functioning white blood cells.
symptoms: Fever, chills, and frequent or persistent infections
Persistent fatigue, weakness, and pale complexion
Easy bruising and frequent bleeding (nosebleeds, bleeding gums)
Tiny red spots on skin (petechiae)
Swollen lymph nodes, enlarged liver or spleen
Unexplained weight loss and drenching night sweats
Bone pain or tenderness
risk_factors: Previous cancer chemotherapy or radiation treatment
Exposure to high levels of radiation or industrial chemicals (e.g., benzene)
Certain genetic disorders (e.g., Down syndrome)
Smoking (for AML)

prefer: Well-cooked, hygienically prepared meals to avoid foodborne infections
High-protein foods (eggs, well-cooked poultry, legumes, pasteurized dairy)
Thoroughly washed, peeled fruits and cooked vegetables
Calorie-dense, nutritious smoothies or soups when appetite is low
limit: Raw or undercooked meats, seafood, sushi, and runny eggs (neutropenic precautions)
Unpasteurized milk, cheeses, and juices
Unwashed raw produce
food.general_tip: Follow strict food hygiene and food safety guidelines to protect against bacterial and viral infections during treatment.

recommended: Short, gentle walks around the home or garden as energy permits
Light stretching and seated range-of-motion exercises
Relaxation breathing exercises
precautions: Avoid crowded gyms and public fitness centers when white blood cell counts are low.
Avoid contact sports or activities with injury risk due to low platelet counts and bleeding risks.
Stop immediately if feeling fatigued, feverish, or dizzy.

lifestyle: Practice strict hand hygiene and wear protective masks in crowded settings
Avoid contact with individuals who have active infections or colds
Prioritize ample sleep and emotional support networks
Maintain clean living spaces
monitoring: Frequent Complete Blood Count (CBC) with differential monitoring
Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration follow-ups
Platelet count and clotting profile assessments
Routine temperature checks for early infection detection
medical_guidance: Undergo care with a specialized hematologist-oncologist.
Adhere strictly to chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy protocols.
Report any fever immediately (fever in neutropenic patients is a medical emergency).
warning_signs: Any fever of 100.4°F (38.0°C) or higher with low white blood cell count
Uncontrolled bleeding from gums, nose, or minor cuts
Sudden, severe shortness of breath or chest pain
Confusion, severe headache, or vision changes
when_to_seek_help: Go to the emergency department IMMEDIATELY for any fever during chemotherapy or with known low white counts.
Seek immediate emergency care for major unexplained bleeding or bruising.

HIV_AIDS.description: Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) attacks the body's immune system, specifically CD4 helper T cells. If left untreated, it can lead to Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS).
symptoms: Early flu-like illness (fever, chills, rash, night sweats, sore throat)
Swollen lymph nodes (especially in neck and groin)
Rapid unexplained weight loss ('wasting')
Recurring fever and profuse night sweats
Chronic diarrhea lasting more than a week
Prolonged fatigue and sores in mouth, anus, or genitals
risk_factors: Unprotected sexual contact without barrier methods or PrEP
Sharing contaminated needles or syringes
Mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy, childbirth, or breastfeeding (without medical intervention)

prefer: Nutrient-dense whole foods, colorful vegetables, and fruits
High-protein sources (lean meats, beans, pasteurized dairy) to prevent muscle loss
Safe, clean, purified drinking water
Well-cooked foods prepared with strict food hygiene
limit: Raw or undercooked meats, eggs, and unpasteurized dairy products
Excessive alcohol and recreational drugs (which weaken immune response)
Sugary and ultra-processed junk food
food.general_tip: Maintain high-calorie, protein-rich nutrition with rigorous food safety to protect against opportunistic gastrointestinal infections.

recommended: Regular moderate aerobic exercise (walking, jogging, swimming)
Progressive resistance training to build and maintain lean muscle mass
Yoga and stretching for flexibility and mental wellness
precautions: Pace workouts according to daily energy levels.
Ensure adequate rest and hydration after physical activity.
Consult your infectious disease clinician before starting intensive regimens.

lifestyle: Consistent daily adherence to Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) to achieve undetectable viral load (U=U)
Practice safer sex with barrier methods
Stay up to date with recommended vaccinations (pneumococcal, flu, hepatitis)
Avoid smoking and illicit substance use
monitoring: Routine CD4 T-cell count tests
HIV viral load testing (aiming for undetectable viral load)
Liver and kidney function screening
Regular screening for co-infections (TB, Hepatitis B/C, STIs)
medical_guidance: Take prescribed Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) every single day at the same time.
Work with an experienced infectious disease specialist.
Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U): an undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission.
warning_signs: Persistent high fever or severe, productive cough (possible opportunistic pneumonia or TB)
Severe, relentless headache with stiff neck or light sensitivity (possible meningitis)
Sudden, severe vision loss or eye pain
Rapid, extreme weight loss and severe chronic diarrhea
when_to_seek_help: Immediate emergency care for high fever, severe breathing difficulty, or altered mental status.
Prompt medical visit for any new rash, mouth ulcers, or unexplained weight loss.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - HIV/AIDS Fact Sheet
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - HIV

Breast_Cancer.description: Breast cancer is a malignancy that originates in the cells of the breast, most commonly forming in the ducts (invasive ductal carcinoma) or the lobules (invasive lobular carcinoma).
symptoms: A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm area
Change in the size, shape, or appearance of the breast
Dimpling, puckering, or redness of the breast skin (orange peel texture)
Nipple inversion, pain, or abnormal discharge (especially bloody)
Scaling, peeling, or flaking of the areola or breast skin
risk_factors: Female gender and increasing age (over 50)
Inherited genetic mutations (BRCA1, BRCA2 genes)
Personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer
Dense breast tissue
Early menstruation (before age 12) or late menopause (after age 55)
Postmenopausal obesity and alcohol consumption

prefer: Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, kale)
Antioxidant-rich berries and citrus fruits
Fiber-rich legumes, flaxseeds, and whole grains
Healthy fats from olive oil, avocados, and fatty fish
limit: Alcoholic beverages (even moderate alcohol increases breast cancer risk)
Charred, overcooked, and processed meats
Excess refined sugars and high-glycemic carbohydrates
Saturated and industrial trans fats
food.general_tip: Maintain a plant-forward, fiber-dense diet and limit alcohol consumption to support cellular health.

recommended: Moderate aerobic activities (brisk walking, cycling, swimming, 150 mins/week)
Strength and resistance training (2 days/week)
Gentle arm and shoulder range-of-motion exercises following surgery
precautions: Work with a certified lymphedema therapist for upper body exercise if lymph nodes were removed.
Wear supportive, well-fitting sports bras.
Avoid heavy strain on surgical sites until fully cleared by the surgical team.

lifestyle: Maintain a healthy body weight, especially after menopause
Limit or avoid alcohol consumption
Perform regular breast self-awareness and attend routine mammograms
Engage in cancer survivorship support groups
monitoring: Regular screening mammography as per clinical guidelines (usually annual or biennial)
Clinical breast examinations by a healthcare professional
Breast MRI or ultrasound for high-risk individuals or dense breasts
Genetic counseling and testing if strong family history exists
medical_guidance: Discuss an individualized screening plan with your gynecologist or primary physician.
Follow prescribed multidisciplinary treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, endocrine therapy).
Do not ignore any new breast change or lump, even if a recent mammogram was normal.
warning_signs: A hard, painless lump with irregular edges in the breast or armpit
Rapid swelling, warmth, and redness of the entire breast (inflammatory signs)
Spontaneous bloody or clear nipple discharge
Skin ulceration or sudden nipple retraction
when_to_seek_help: Schedule a prompt clinical evaluation whenever any new breast lump, skin dimple, or nipple change is noticed.
Seek immediate medical attention for signs of post-operative infection (fever, spreading redness, purulent drainage).
sources: National Cancer Institute (NCI) - Breast Cancer Overview
World Health Organization (WHO) - Global Breast Cancer Initiative

Lung_Cancer.description: Lung cancer is a malignant tumor characterized by uncontrolled cell growth in the tissues of the lung, primarily originating in the bronchi, bronchioles, or alveoli.
common_types: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC - Adenocarcinoma, Squamous Cell, Large Cell)
symptoms: A persistent cough that does not go away or gets worse
Coughing up blood or rust-colored phlegm (hemoptysis)
Chest pain that worsens with deep breathing, coughing, or laughing
Hoarseness and voice changes
Shortness of breath and new wheezing
Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
Repeated respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia
risk_factors: Cigarette smoking and exposure to secondhand smoke (primary risk factor)
Exposure to radon gas in homes and buildings
Occupational exposure to asbestos, arsenic, chromium, and diesel exhaust
Family history of lung cancer
Air pollution and particulate matter exposure

prefer: Colorful fruits and vegetables rich in carotenoids and flavonoids
High-calorie, protein-dense foods to prevent cancer cachexia
Hydrating soups, broths, and purees if swallowing is uncomfortable
Small, frequent meals throughout the day
limit: High-dose synthetic beta-carotene supplements (shown to increase risk in active smokers)
Processed and charred meats
Sugary, nutrient-depleted snacks
food.general_tip: Focus on nutrient-dense, easily consumable foods to maintain energy and support lung tissue.

recommended: Pulmonary rehabilitation and breathing retraining exercises
Gentle walking on flat surfaces at a comfortable pace
Seated stretching and light resistance band movements
precautions: Use supplemental oxygen during exercise if prescribed by your pulmonologist.
Stop exercising immediately if experiencing severe shortness of breath or dizziness.
Avoid exercising outdoors on days with poor air quality or high smog.

lifestyle: Completely stop smoking immediately (benefits occur at any stage of diagnosis)
Test your home for radon levels
Avoid secondhand smoke and workplace dust/fume exposure
Use air purifiers indoors
monitoring: Low-Dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) annual screening for eligible high-risk smokers
Chest CT/PET scans during and after oncology treatment
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) and pulse oximetry monitoring
medical_guidance: Work with a thoracic oncologist, pulmonologist, and thoracic surgeon.
Explore molecular biomarker and genetic testing (EGFR, ALK, PD-L1) for targeted therapies.
Attend regular pulmonary rehabilitation sessions.
warning_signs: Coughing up significant amounts of blood
Sudden, severe shortness of breath or inability to catch breath
Swelling of the face, neck, and upper chest (Superior Vena Cava syndrome)
Severe, intractable bone pain or neurological deficits (headache, seizures)
when_to_seek_help: Seek emergency care for sudden severe respiratory distress or coughing up frank blood.
Consult a doctor promptly if a cough persists for more than 3 to 4 weeks.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Lung Cancer

Cervical_Cancer.description: Cervical cancer develops in the cervix (the lower part of the uterus that connects to the vagina), almost always caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV).
symptoms: Abnormal vaginal bleeding (between periods, after intercourse, or postmenopausal)
Unusual, watery, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge
Pelvic pain or pain during sexual intercourse
Lower back pain or leg swelling (in advanced stages)
risk_factors: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV strains (e.g., HPV 16, 18)
Lack of regular Pap smear / HPV screening
Smoking (doubles the risk of cervical cancer)
Weakened immune system (e.g., HIV infection)
Long-term use of oral contraceptives without screening

prefer: Folate-rich foods (dark green leafy vegetables, chickpeas, avocados)
Vitamin A, C, and E rich foods (carrots, bell peppers, berries)
Cruciferous vegetables containing indole-3-carbinol
Plenty of clean water
limit: Processed meats and high-saturated fat foods
Excessive sugar and refined carbohydrates
Alcohol and tobacco products
food.general_tip: Consume an antioxidant-rich, folate-abundant diet to support cervical cellular health and immune defense.

recommended: Regular moderate aerobic exercise (walking, swimming, light cycling)
Pelvic floor physical therapy and gentle core strengthening
Yoga and relaxation techniques for pelvic tension
precautions: Avoid high-impact jumping if experiencing pelvic discomfort.
Follow surgeon's restrictions after cervical biopsy, LEEP, or surgery regarding strenuous activity.

lifestyle: Get vaccinated against HPV (recommended for adolescents and eligible adults up to age 45)
Attend regular cervical cancer screenings (Pap smears and HPV DNA testing)
Avoid tobacco smoking
Practice safer sex using barrier methods
monitoring: Routine Pap smear (every 3 years) or co-testing with HPV DNA (every 5 years) as advised
Colposcopy and cervical biopsy for abnormal screening findings
Post-treatment pelvic examinations and oncologic imaging
medical_guidance: Follow national screening guidelines according to age and risk profile.
Discuss HPV vaccination with your healthcare provider.
Promptly follow up on any abnormal Pap smear or positive HPV result.
warning_signs: Heavy, continuous postmenopausal vaginal bleeding
Severe pelvic pain radiating down the legs
Difficulty or pain during urination accompanied by blood in urine
Unexplained rapid weight loss and persistent fatigue
when_to_seek_help: Seek medical evaluation promptly for any abnormal, unexpected vaginal bleeding or postcoital bleeding.
Consult your gynecologist immediately for severe, persistent pelvic pain.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Cervical Cancer Fact Sheet
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Cervical Cancer

Skin_Cancer.description: Skin cancer is the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of skin cells, most commonly caused by exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight or tanning beds.
symptoms: A new mole or a change in an existing mole (ABCDE rule: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color changes, Diameter >6mm, Evolving)
A pearly or waxy bump on sun-exposed skin (face, ears, neck)
A firm, red nodule or flat lesion with a scaly, crusted surface
A sore that does not heal, bleeds, or oozes repeatedly
Dark lesions under fingernails or on palms/soles
risk_factors: Excessive exposure to UV sunlight and history of sunburns
Use of indoor tanning beds
Fair skin, light hair, light eyes, and freckles
Large number of moles or presence of atypical (dysplastic) moles
Weakened immune system or family history of melanoma

prefer: Antioxidant-dense foods (blueberries, tomatoes with lycopene, leafy greens)
Omega-3 fatty acids (flaxseeds, walnuts, wild salmon)
Green tea containing polyphenols (EGCG)
Adequate water to support skin hydration
limit: Excessive alcohol consumption
Ultra-processed foods and artificial trans fats
Refined sugars and high-glycemic snacks
food.general_tip: Incorporate antioxidant and polyphenol-rich foods into your daily diet to support cellular DNA repair mechanisms.

recommended: Indoor fitness activities, gym workouts, or swimming in covered pools
Outdoor walking and running scheduled before 10:00 AM or after 4:00 PM
Yoga, Pilates, and bodyweight training
precautions: Apply broad-spectrum SPF 30+ water-resistant sunscreen 20 minutes before outdoor exercise.
Wear UV-protective clothing (UPF 50+), wide-brimmed hats, and UV-blocking sunglasses.
Reapply sunscreen every 2 hours or immediately after heavy sweating or swimming.

lifestyle: Never use tanning beds or UV sun lamps
Seek shade during peak UV hours (10:00 AM to 4:00 PM)
Perform monthly head-to-toe skin self-examinations using a full-length mirror
Wear protective clothing, long sleeves, and broad-brimmed hats outdoors
monitoring: Monthly skin self-checks following the ABCDE criteria
Annual comprehensive total-body skin examination by a certified dermatologist
Dermoscopy and digital mole mapping for high-risk individuals
medical_guidance: Visit a board-certified dermatologist for any suspicious or changing spot.
Have any biopsy-confirmed skin cancer treated promptly according to stage.
Never attempt to scratch, freeze, or remove moles at home.
warning_signs: A mole changing rapidly in size, color, shape, or height
A mole that itches, burns, tingles, or bleeds spontaneously
A dark spot with irregular borders and multiple shades of brown, black, blue, or red
A non-healing ulcer or crusted bump persisting longer than 4 weeks
when_to_seek_help: Schedule an urgent dermatology appointment for any mole meeting the ABCDE warning signs.
Consult a doctor for any new, persistent, or rapidly growing skin growth.

Colorectal_Cancer.description: Colorectal cancer is a malignancy that begins in the large intestine (colon) or rectum, typically originating as noncancerous polyps (adenomas) that slowly transform into cancer over time.
symptoms: A persistent change in bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or narrowing of stool)
Rectal bleeding or dark blood in the stool
Persistent abdominal discomfort, cramping, gas, or pain
A feeling that the bowel does not empty completely
Weakness, unexplained fatigue, and iron deficiency anemia
Unexplained weight loss
risk_factors: Age 50 and older (though rates in young adults are rising)
Personal or family history of colorectal polyps or cancer
Inherited syndromes (Lynch syndrome, Familial Adenomatous Polyposis)
Inflammatory bowel disease (Ulcerative Colitis or Crohn's disease)
Sedentary lifestyle, obesity, smoking, and heavy alcohol use
Diet high in red and processed meats and low in fiber

prefer: High-fiber foods (beans, lentils, oats, whole wheat, vegetables)
Calcium and Vitamin D rich foods (fortified dairy/plant milk, leafy greens)
Antioxidant-rich fruits (apples, berries, oranges)
Plenty of water to maintain digestive regularity
limit: Processed meats (hot dogs, sausages, bacon, deli meats)
Excessive red meat (beef, pork, lamb)
Alcoholic beverages
Ultra-processed low-fiber foods
food.general_tip: Adopt a high-fiber, plant-rich diet and minimize processed meats to support colorectal health.

recommended: Brisk walking, jogging, or cycling (at least 150-300 mins/week)
Core and abdominal strengthening routines
Moderate resistance training
precautions: Start gradually if recovering from abdominal surgery or ostomy placement.
Stay well hydrated before, during, and after workouts.
Consult with your surgical or oncology team regarding hernia precautions.

lifestyle: Maintain a healthy body weight and waist circumference
Quit smoking and avoid all tobacco products
Limit or eliminate alcohol consumption
Stay physically active every day
monitoring: Routine screening colonoscopy starting at age 45 (or earlier for high-risk individuals)
Stool-based screening tests (FIT, fecal occult blood, FIT-DNA) where indicated
Carcinoembryonic Antigen (CEA) blood tests during oncology surveillance
medical_guidance: Adhere to recommended colorectal cancer screening guidelines.
Have precancerous polyps removed promptly during colonoscopy.
Report persistent changes in bowel habits or visible blood in stool to a gastroenterologist.
warning_signs: Significant bright red blood from the rectum or dark, tarry stools
Severe, persistent abdominal pain and swelling
Complete bowel obstruction (inability to pass stool or gas accompanied by vomiting)
Severe, unexplained weakness from rapid drop in hemoglobin
when_to_seek_help: Seek emergency evaluation for severe abdominal pain, vomiting, or heavy rectal bleeding.
Schedule a gastroenterology appointment promptly for persistent bowel habit changes or blood in stool.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Colorectal Cancer

Gastric_Cancer.description: Gastric (stomach) cancer is a malignancy that develops from the cells lining the stomach wall, most commonly in the inner glandular mucosa.
symptoms: Persistent indigestion, heartburn, or stomach discomfort
Feeling full after eating only small amounts of food (early satiety)
Persistent nausea and vomiting (sometimes with blood)
Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
Difficulty or pain while swallowing (dysphagia)
Vague abdominal pain above the navel
Dark, tarry stools (melena)
risk_factors: Chronic Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) bacterial infection
Diet high in smoked, salted, pickled foods and low in fresh fruits/vegetables
Tobacco smoking and heavy alcohol use
Chronic atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, or gastric polyps
Family history or hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1 gene mutation)

prefer: Fresh fruits rich in Vitamin C (citrus, melons, berries)
Fresh green vegetables and whole grains
Small, frequent, easy-to-digest meals
Lean proteins (poached poultry, soft eggs, tofu, fish)
limit: Smoked, cured, salted, and pickled foods
Charred, grilled meats and processed sausages
Excessive spicy, acidic, or extremely hot foods
Alcohol and tobacco
food.general_tip: Choose freshly prepared, nutrient-dense, easily digestible foods and avoid heavily salted, smoked, or preserved items.

recommended: Light walking after meals to aid gastric motility
Gentle stretching and mobility exercises
Relaxation breathing routines
precautions: Avoid vigorous exercise immediately following large meals.
Pace physical activity around treatment-related fatigue and caloric intake.
Follow dietary and hydration recommendations before workouts.

lifestyle: Quit smoking and avoid secondhand smoke
Maintain good food hygiene and drink clean, tested water
Get tested and treated for H. pylori infection if experiencing chronic gastritis
Eat smaller meals more frequently throughout the day
monitoring: Upper endoscopy (EGD) with tissue biopsy for diagnosis and surveillance
H. pylori testing and post-treatment eradication confirmation
Complete blood counts to monitor for chronic blood loss anemia
medical_guidance: Undergo care with a surgical oncologist and gastroenterologist.
Follow specialized dietary plans if undergoing partial or total gastrectomy.
Never ignore chronic indigestion that persists despite standard antacid use.
warning_signs: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground like material
Black, tarry, sticky stools
Complete inability to swallow food or liquids
Severe, worsening abdominal pain and extreme cachexia
when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate emergency care for vomiting blood or passing black tarry stools.
Consult a gastroenterologist for persistent stomach pain, early satiety, or difficulty swallowing.

Chronic_Kidney_Disease.description: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a gradual, progressive loss of kidney function over time, leading to the accumulation of waste products and fluid in the body.
symptoms: Fatigue, low energy, and poor concentration
Swelling in the feet, ankles, legs, or hands (edema)
Puffiness around the eyes (especially in the morning)
Changes in urination frequency (especially nocturia)
Foamy, bubbly, or dark urine
Persistent itchy, dry skin
Muscle cramps and metallic taste in the mouth
risk_factors: Diabetes (leading cause of CKD)
High blood pressure (hypertension)
Cardiovascular disease
Family history of kidney disease
Chronic use of NSAID pain relievers (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen)
Polycystic kidney disease or glomerulonephritis

prefer: Fresh fruits and vegetables tailored to individualized potassium allowances
Healthy cooking oils (olive oil)
High-quality, portion-controlled protein sources
Low-sodium home-cooked foods flavored with herbs
limit: Excess sodium and table salt
High-phosphorus foods (colass, processed cheeses, packaged meats)
High-potassium foods if potassium levels are elevated (bananas, potatoes, tomatoes)
Excessive protein intake in advanced CKD stages (unless on dialysis)
food.general_tip: Work with a specialized renal dietitian to customize sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and protein targets based on your CKD stage.

recommended: Moderate walking, stationary cycling, and water aerobics (30 mins/day, 5 days/week)
Low-resistance strength training
Flexibility and balance exercises
precautions: Avoid extreme high-intensity workouts that cause severe muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis).
Stay within recommended fluid restriction guidelines while exercising.
Check blood pressure before and after physical activity.

lifestyle: Strictly control blood pressure (target usually <130/80 mmHg as advised)
Maintain tight blood sugar control if diabetic
Avoid over-the-counter NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) without nephrologist consent
Quit smoking and maintain a healthy weight
monitoring: Routine estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) and serum creatinine tests
Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (uACR) testing
Electrolytes (potassium, sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphorus) monitoring
Frequent blood pressure tracking
medical_guidance: Partner closely with a nephrologist and renal care team.
Take prescribed ACE inhibitors, ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, or other kidney-protective medications as directed.
Understand your lab numbers (eGFR, uACR, potassium) and their trends.
warning_signs: Severe shortness of breath from fluid accumulation in lungs (pulmonary edema)
Marked decrease or complete cessation of urine output
Severe confusion, drowsiness, or seizures (uremic encephalopathy)
Chest pain or irregular heartbeat from dangerously high potassium (hyperkalemia)
when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate emergency care for severe breathlessness, chest pain, or marked fluid retention.
Contact your nephrologist promptly if blood pressure is dangerously high or urine output drops noticeably.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Chronic Kidney Disease

Obesity.description: Obesity is a complex, chronic relapsing disease characterized by excess adiposity (body fat) that impairs health and increases the risk of numerous metabolic and cardiovascular conditions.
common_types: Class 3 Obesity (BMI 40.0 or higher / Severe Obesity)
symptoms: Excess body fat accumulation around abdomen and vital organs
Breathlessness during light exertion
Joint and back pain from increased mechanical load
Excessive sweating and heat intolerance
Daytime fatigue and loud snoring / obstructive sleep apnea
Skin irritation and friction rashes in skin folds
risk_factors: Dietary habits high in ultra-processed, energy-dense foods and sugary beverages
Sedentary lifestyle and lack of regular physical activity
Genetic factors and family history
Hormonal imbalances, chronic stress, and sleep deprivation
Certain medications (steroids, antidepressants, antipsychotics)

prefer: Whole, minimally processed foods (vegetables, legumes, whole grains)
Lean proteins (chicken breast, fish, tofu, beans) to promote satiety
High-fiber foods that slow digestion and stabilize blood sugar
Water as the primary beverage
limit: Sugar-sweetened sodas, energy drinks, and fruit juices
Fast foods, deep-fried snacks, and pastries
Highly refined grains and white flour products
Excessive alcohol intake
food.general_tip: Focus on sustainable, nutrient-dense whole foods and portion control rather than severe crash dieting.

recommended: Gradual progression to 150-300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week (walking, cycling, swimming)
Resistance and strength training (2-3 days per week) to preserve lean muscle mass
Water aerobics and low-impact movements to minimize joint strain
precautions: Choose low-impact activities to protect knees, hips, and lower back.
Warm up and cool down thoroughly to prevent musculoskeletal injuries.
Stay hydrated and avoid overheating during exercise.

lifestyle: Target 7-9 hours of quality sleep per night (sleep debt alters appetite hormones)
Practice mindful eating and stress management techniques
Track daily physical activity using a pedometer or smartwatch
Build a supportive network of family, friends, or healthcare coaches
monitoring: Regular monitoring of body weight, waist circumference, and BMI
Routine fasting glucose, HbA1c, and lipid panel screenings
Blood pressure checks and screening for obstructive sleep apnea
Liver function tests (to screen for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease)
medical_guidance: Work collaboratively with an obesity medicine specialist, primary care physician, and registered dietitian.
Discuss medically supervised lifestyle interventions, anti-obesity pharmacotherapy, or metabolic bariatric surgery if appropriate.
Focus on overall metabolic health gains rather than solely on scale weight.
warning_signs: Sudden chest pain, tightness, or severe shortness of breath
Episodes of gasping for air or waking with a choke during sleep
Severe joint swelling and sudden inability to bear weight
Pain, warmth, and swelling in one calf (possible deep vein thrombosis)
when_to_seek_help: Seek emergency care for chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or one-sided leg swelling.
Consult a physician to develop an individualized, comprehensive medical weight management plan.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Obesity and Overweight
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Adult Obesity

Thyroid_Disease.description: Thyroid disease encompasses disorders affecting the thyroid gland, leading to either insufficient hormone production (hypothyroidism) or excessive hormone production (hyperthyroidism).
symptoms: Hypothyroidism: Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, hair thinning
Hyperthyroidism: Unexplained weight loss, rapid heartbeat, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremors, insomnia
Enlarged neck swelling (goiter) or difficulty swallowing
risk_factors: Female gender (women are 5 to 8 times more likely to develop thyroid disorders)
Personal or family history of autoimmune diseases (Type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, vitiligo)
Past radiation exposure to neck or head
Postpartum period or recent pregnancy
Inadequate or excessive dietary iodine intake

prefer: Adequate dietary iodine (iodized salt, seafood, dairy in balanced amounts)
Selenium-rich foods (Brazil nuts, sunflower seeds, tuna)
Zinc-rich foods (pumpkin seeds, lentils, lean poultry)
Anti-inflammatory whole foods and fiber
limit: Excessive raw cruciferous vegetables (cabbage, kale) if iodine deficient
Soy products and high-calcium foods taken within 4 hours of thyroid hormone medication
Excessive kelp or high-dose iodine supplements without medical guidance
food.general_tip: Maintain a balanced, nutrient-dense diet; separate thyroid hormone medication (e.g. levothyroxine) from calcium, iron, and soy supplements by at least 4 hours.

recommended: Moderate aerobic activities (walking, cycling, swimming)
Strength and resistance training to boost metabolic rate
Yoga and relaxation techniques for stress reduction
precautions: In hyperthyroidism, avoid strenuous high-heart-rate exercise until hormone levels are controlled.
In hypothyroidism, start exercise slowly to accommodate fatigue and muscle stiffness.
Stay hydrated and avoid extreme temperature environments.

lifestyle: Take thyroid replacement medication consistently on an empty stomach with a full glass of water 30-60 minutes before breakfast
Manage psychological stress (stress influences endocrine function)
Prioritize consistent, restful sleep
Avoid smoking (smoking worsens thyroid eye disease)
monitoring: Regular Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T4, Free T3)
Thyroid autoantibody tests (anti-TPO, anti-Tg, TSI)
Thyroid ultrasound imaging for nodules or goiter
medical_guidance: Work with an endocrinologist or primary care physician.
Keep medication dosage consistent and never alter doses without repeat lab tests.
Attend regular follow-up blood tests every 6 to 12 weeks after dosage adjustments.
warning_signs: Severe, rapid heart rate (>120 bpm), high fever, and delirium (Thyroid Storm)
Extreme hypothermia, profound lethargy, and slowed breathing (Myxedema Coma)
Protrusion, redness, and severe pain in the eyes (Thyroid Eye Disease)
Rapidly enlarging hard neck lump with hoarseness
when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate emergency medical attention for symptoms of thyroid storm or myxedema coma.
Consult your doctor if you experience persistent palpitations, severe heat/cold intolerance, or rapid weight fluctuations.
