PCOS.description: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is a common hormonal disorder characterized by irregular menstrual cycles, excess androgen (male hormone) levels, and polycystic ovarian morphology.
symptoms: Irregular, infrequent, or absent menstrual periods
Excess facial and body hair growth (hirsutism)
Severe adult acne and oily skin
Thinning hair on the scalp (female pattern hair loss)
Weight gain and difficulty losing weight
Darkened skin patches in neck creases and underarms (acanthosis nigricans)
Infertility or difficulty conceiving
risk_factors: Insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia
Family history of PCOS or Type 2 diabetes
Chronic low-grade inflammation
Overweight or obesity

prefer: Low-glycemic index foods (quinoa, barley, sweet potatoes, legumes)
Anti-inflammatory foods (berries, tomatoes, fatty fish, leafy greens)
High-fiber vegetables and lean proteins with every meal
Healthy fats from nuts, seeds, and extra virgin olive oil
limit: Refined carbohydrates (white bread, pastries, sugary breakfast cereals)
Sugar-sweetened beverages and high-fructose corn syrup
Processed and fried foods that exacerbate inflammation
Excessive dairy if found to aggravate personal acne symptoms
food.general_tip: Focus on low-glycemic, anti-inflammatory whole foods to stabilize insulin levels and balance hormones.

recommended: Resistance and strength training (3 days per week to improve insulin sensitivity)
Moderate-intensity interval training (HIIT) or brisk walking
Pilates, yoga, and gentle stretching for cortisol reduction
precautions: Avoid excessive, chronic over-training which can spike cortisol and worsen hormonal imbalances.
Allow adequate rest and recovery days between intense workouts.

lifestyle: Prioritize consistent 7-8 hours of quality sleep to optimize insulin regulation
Implement daily stress management practices (meditation, journaling)
Maintain regular physical movement throughout the day
Track menstrual cycles and symptoms using a dedicated log
monitoring: Hormonal panel testing (Total/Free Testosterone, DHEA-S, LH, FSH, Prolactin)
Fasting glucose, insulin, and oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT)
Lipid panel screening
Pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian morphology and endometrial thickness
medical_guidance: Work with a gynecologist, reproductive endocrinologist, and dietitian.
Discuss personalized strategies for cycle regulation, fertility, and metabolic health.
Screen regularly for diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and sleep apnea.
warning_signs: Absence of menstrual periods for >3 consecutive months without pregnancy (risk of endometrial hyperplasia)
Extremely heavy, prolonged bleeding causing severe dizziness or pallor
Sudden, severe pelvic pain (possible ovarian cyst rupture or torsion)
Severe depressive symptoms or anxiety
when_to_seek_help: Seek urgent care for sudden, severe sharp pelvic pain or heavy bleeding causing weakness.
Consult your gynecologist for irregular cycles, fertility concerns, or persistent signs of androgen excess.
sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) - PCOS
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guidelines on PCOS
World Health Organization (WHO) - Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

Osteoporosis.description: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal condition characterized by low bone mass, microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, and an increased susceptibility to fragility fractures.
common_types: Secondary Osteoporosis (due to medications, malabsorption, or chronic conditions)
Osteopenia (low bone mass / precursor to osteoporosis)
symptoms: Often called a 'silent disease' with no symptoms until a bone fractures
Loss of height over time (1 inch or more)
Stooped or hunched posture (kyphosis / 'dowager's hump')
Sudden, severe back pain caused by a fractured or collapsed vertebra
Bone fractures occurring from minor bumps or simple falls from standing height
risk_factors: Postmenopausal women and advancing age (over 65)
Low body weight or small body frame
Family history of osteoporosis or hip fracture
Long-term use of corticosteroid medications (prednisone)
Inadequate dietary calcium and Vitamin D intake
Sedentary lifestyle, smoking, and heavy alcohol intake

prefer: Calcium-rich foods (dairy products, fortified plant milk, tofu, collard greens, canned sardines with bones)
Vitamin D sources (fatty fish, egg yolks, fortified cereals)
Magnesium and Vitamin K2 sources (leafy greens, nuts, fermented foods)
Adequate lean protein to maintain muscle mass
limit: Excessive sodium (increases calcium excretion in urine)
Excessive alcohol (impairs bone remodeling and increases fall risk)
High consumption of caffeinated energy drinks and colas
Smoking
food.general_tip: Ensure adequate daily intake of calcium (1,000-1,200 mg) and Vitamin D (800-2,000 IU) through balanced dietary sources and clinician-approved supplements.

recommended: Weight-bearing aerobic exercises (brisk walking, low-impact aerobics, stair climbing)
Progressive resistance training with weights or bands (2-3 days/week)
Balance and stability exercises (Tai Chi, single-leg stands) to prevent falls
precautions: Avoid high-impact jumping, running, or sudden jarring movements.
Avoid loaded spinal flexion (touching toes, crunches) and extreme spinal twisting.
Exercise in a safe environment with non-slip flooring.

lifestyle: Fall-proof your home (remove loose rugs, improve lighting, install bathroom grab bars)
Wear stable, low-heeled shoes with non-slip rubber soles
Completely quit smoking and limit alcohol intake
Maintain adequate sun exposure safely for Vitamin D synthesis
monitoring: Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) bone density scans (T-score evaluation)
FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool) score calculations
Serum 25-hydroxy Vitamin D, calcium, and kidney function tests
medical_guidance: Discuss bone density test results and fracture risk with your physician.
Take prescribed antiresorptive or bone-anabolic medications (e.g., bisphosphonates) exactly as instructed.
Never ignore sudden severe back pain following minor movements.
warning_signs: Sudden, severe back pain following minor bending or lifting (possible vertebral compression fracture)
Inability to stand or bear weight after a minor fall
Severe hip, groin, or wrist pain with visible deformity
when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate emergency medical evaluation after any fall with suspected bone fracture.
Consult your doctor for bone density screening if you are a woman over 65, a man over 70, or have high risk factors.
sources: National Osteoporosis Foundation (Bone Health & Osteoporosis Foundation - BHOF)
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Osteoporosis

Pneumonia.description: Pneumonia is an acute inflammatory infection of one or both lungs, where the air sacs (alveoli) fill with fluid or pus, causing cough, fever, chills, and difficulty breathing.
symptoms: Cough producing green, yellow, or bloody phlegm
High fever, sweating, and shaking chills
Sharp or stabbing chest pain that worsens when breathing deeply or coughing
Shortness of breath and rapid, shallow breathing
Fatigue, loss of appetite, and nausea
Confusion or altered mental state, especially in older adults
risk_factors: Age extremes (children under 2 and adults 65 or older)
Chronic lung conditions (COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis)
Weakened immune system (HIV, chemotherapy, immunosuppressants)
Tobacco smoking and environmental air pollution
Recent viral respiratory infection (flu, COVID-19)

prefer: Warm, hydrating broths, herbal teas, and soups
Plenty of clean water and electrolyte fluids
Nutrient-dense fruits rich in Vitamin C (berries, oranges)
Easily digestible proteins (poached poultry, soft eggs, lentils)
limit: Dairy products if they make mucus feel uncomfortably thicker for the individual
Cold drinks and caffeinated beverages
Sugary, processed, heavy foods
Alcohol and tobacco
food.general_tip: Maintain high fluid intake and warm, soothing broths to loosen respiratory secretions and prevent dehydration.

recommended: Complete physical rest during the acute infection phase
Deep breathing and incentive spirometry exercises in bed
Gradual, short indoor walking only after fever subsides and energy returns
precautions: Do not engage in moderate or vigorous exercise until fully recovered and cleared by a clinician.
Avoid exposure to cold, dry air.
Rest immediately if breathing becomes labored.

lifestyle: Prioritize extensive bed rest and sleep
Use a cool-mist humidifier in the bedroom
Avoid all exposure to tobacco smoke and chemical fumes
Stay up to date with pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccinations
monitoring: Pulse oximetry monitoring (blood oxygen saturation should ideally be 95% or higher)
Body temperature tracking
Chest X-ray to confirm resolution of consolidation
Sputum and blood cultures if hospitalized
medical_guidance: Seek prompt medical diagnosis and follow prescribed antimicrobial or supportive care.
Complete the full course of prescribed antibiotics if bacterial pneumonia is diagnosed.
Attend scheduled medical follow-up visits to ensure lungs are fully clear.
warning_signs: Oxygen saturation dropping below 92% on room air
Severe shortness of breath, gasping, or inability to speak in sentences
Bluish lips or fingertips (cyanosis)
Confusion, severe dizziness, or persistent high fever unresponsive to medication
when_to_seek_help: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency care for severe breathing difficulty, low oxygen, cyanosis, or confusion.
Visit a doctor promptly for high fever, productive cough, and sharp chest pain.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Pneumonia in Children and Adults
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Pneumonia

Tuberculosis.description: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs (pulmonary TB) but capable of spreading to other organs.
common_types: Extrapulmonary TB (lymph nodes, bones, kidneys, brain)
symptoms: A bad cough lasting 3 weeks or longer
Coughing up blood or sputum (hemoptysis)
Chest pain when breathing or coughing
Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite
Prolonged fever and drenching night sweats
Persistent fatigue and weakness
risk_factors: Close contact with someone who has active pulmonary TB
Weakened immune system (HIV infection, malnutrition, diabetes, chemotherapy)
Living or working in high-density or crowded settings
Substance abuse and tobacco smoking
Living in or traveling to regions with high TB prevalence

prefer: Calorie-dense and high-protein foods (eggs, legumes, fish, dairy) to counteract wasting
Vitamin A, B-complex, C, D, and E rich foods
Zinc and iron rich foods (nuts, seeds, leafy greens)
Frequent small meals rich in healthy fats
limit: Alcohol (crucial to avoid as TB medications are metabolized by the liver)
Excessive caffeine and sugary sodas
Tobacco products
food.general_tip: Emphasize high-calorie, protein-rich nutrition with total avoidance of alcohol to support immune recovery and protect liver health.

recommended: Strict rest during the initial infectious and symptomatic phases
Gentle breathing exercises and short walks as energy returns and after becoming non-infectious
Gradual progressive rehabilitation
precautions: Do not engage in strenuous exertion while actively ill or fatigued.
Exercise only in private or well-ventilated spaces until confirmed non-contagious.
Stop immediately if experiencing chest pain or breathlessness.

lifestyle: Strict adherence to Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) for the full 6-9 month medication duration
Wear a high-filtration mask (N95) around others during the infectious period
Ensure excellent room ventilation (open windows, sunlight exposure)
Strictly abstain from alcohol and smoking
monitoring: Monthly sputum smear and culture tests until consecutive negative results are confirmed
Serial chest X-rays to assess lung healing
Routine Liver Function Tests (LFTs - ALT, AST, Bilirubin) to monitor drug toxicity
Periodic vision and hearing checks (for specific second-line TB drugs)
medical_guidance: Work with public health authorities and infectious disease specialists.
NEVER stop or miss doses of TB medications, even when feeling completely healthy (prevents drug resistance).
Ensure household contacts are screened for latent or active TB.
warning_signs: Coughing up large quantities of frank blood (massive hemoptysis)
Severe shortness of breath or sudden chest pain
Yellowing of the eyes/skin, severe nausea, or dark urine (signs of drug-induced liver injury)
Severe, persistent vomiting or numbness/tingling in hands and feet
when_to_seek_help: Seek emergency medical care for massive hemoptysis, jaundice, or severe breathlessness.
Report any missed medication doses or side effects immediately to your TB clinic.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Tuberculosis Global Report
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Tuberculosis

Asthma.description: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways characterized by hyperresponsiveness, bronchospasm, and mucus production, leading to recurrent episodes of wheezing and breathlessness.
symptoms: Recurrent wheezing (a whistling sound when exhaling)
Shortness of breath and rapid breathing
Chest tightness or pain
Persistent coughing, especially at night or early morning
Trouble sleeping caused by coughing or wheezing
risk_factors: Family history of asthma or allergic conditions (atopy)
Personal history of allergic rhinitis (hay fever) or eczema
Exposure to environmental triggers (pollen, dust mites, pet dander, mold)
Tobacco smoke exposure (active and secondhand)
Occupational fumes, chemicals, and outdoor air pollution

prefer: Antioxidant-rich fresh fruits (apples, berries, citrus) and vegetables
Omega-3 fatty acids (salmon, flaxseeds, walnuts) to reduce inflammation
Magnesium-rich foods (spinach, pumpkin seeds, whole grains)
Adequate water hydration
limit: Foods containing sulfites and preservatives (dried fruits, wine, pickled foods)
Known personal food allergens (e.g., shellfish, peanuts, dairy if allergic)
Excessive sodium and processed fast foods
food.general_tip: Follow an anti-inflammatory dietary pattern rich in fresh produce and avoid foods with sulfites or known allergy triggers.

recommended: Swimming and water sports (humid, warm air is gentle on airways)
Walking, gentle cycling, and hiking in mild weather
Yoga, diaphragmatic breathing, and Pranayama routines
precautions: Always carry a prescribed quick-relief rescue inhaler (e.g., albuterol) during exercise.
Warm up and cool down thoroughly for 10-15 minutes.
Avoid outdoor workouts in cold, dry weather or on days with high pollen/pollution counts.

lifestyle: Identify and avoid individual asthma triggers (dust mites, pet dander, mold, tobacco smoke)
Use allergen-proof mattress and pillow covers
Maintain indoor humidity below 50% to prevent mold and dust mites
Keep a peak flow meter and Asthma Action Plan readily accessible
monitoring: Daily or periodic Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) monitoring
Spirometry (FEV1, FVC) assessments during clinical checkups
Tracking symptom frequency and rescue inhaler usage (rule of twos)
medical_guidance: Develop a written Asthma Action Plan with your pulmonologist or allergist.
Use daily controller/preventer inhalers consistently even when symptom-free.
Know the difference between daily controller medications and fast-acting rescue inhalers.
warning_signs: Severe breathlessness and inability to speak in full sentences
Rescue inhaler provides no relief or lasts less than 2-3 hours
Ribs or neck muscles pulling in tightly during breathing (retractions)
Peak flow reading in the 'Red Zone' (<50% of personal best)
Bluish color in lips or fingernails (cyanosis)
when_to_seek_help: Call emergency services immediately for an acute, severe asthma attack not responding to rescue medication.
Contact your doctor if you need your rescue inhaler more than twice a week for daytime symptoms.
sources: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI / NIH) Guidelines

COPD.description: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a progressive, chronic inflammatory lung disease that causes obstructed airflow from the lungs, primarily comprising emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
common_types: Chronic Bronchitis (chronic inflammation and mucus in bronchial tubes)
symptoms: Shortness of breath (dyspnea), especially during physical activities
Chronic cough that produces significant mucus/sputum
Frequent respiratory infections (colds, bronchitis, pneumonia)
Wheezing and chest tightness
Lack of energy and progressive limitation in daily activities
Unintended weight loss in advanced stages
risk_factors: Long-term tobacco smoking (primary cause in 85-90% of cases)
Long-term occupational exposure to dusts, chemicals, and industrial fumes
Exposure to indoor biomass fuel smoke and outdoor air pollution
Genetic deficiency of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AATD)
History of severe childhood respiratory infections

prefer: High-protein, calorie-dense foods to prevent muscle wasting and respiratory muscle fatigue
Antioxidant-rich vegetables and fruits
Healthy fats (avocados, nuts, olive oil) which produce less CO2 per calorie metabolized than carbohydrates
Small, frequent meals to prevent diaphragm crowding
limit: Excessive simple carbohydrates and sugary sodas (which increase carbon dioxide production)
Excess sodium (can cause fluid retention and breathing difficulty)
Gas-producing foods that cause bloating and push against the diaphragm
Alcohol and tobacco
food.general_tip: Eat small, frequent, nutrient-dense meals high in healthy fats and proteins; rest before eating to conserve energy.

recommended: Structured Pulmonary Rehabilitation programs
Pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing training
Gentle walking on flat surfaces with scheduled rest intervals
Upper-body resistance band exercises to strengthen breathing muscles
precautions: Use portable supplemental oxygen during exercise if prescribed.
Stop immediately if experiencing extreme shortness of breath, dizziness, or chest pain.
Avoid exercising outdoors during extreme cold, high heat, or poor air quality.

lifestyle: Completely quit smoking immediately (the single most effective intervention to slow decline)
Stay up to date with pneumococcal, influenza, and COVID-19 vaccines
Use air purifiers and maintain clean indoor air
Practice energy-saving techniques during daily chores
monitoring: Periodic Spirometry testing (FEV1/FVC post-bronchodilator ratio)
Pulse oximetry and arterial blood gas (ABG) measurements
Tracking frequency of acute COPD exacerbations
Alpha-1 Antitrypsin genetic testing in newly diagnosed individuals
medical_guidance: Work closely with a pulmonologist and respiratory therapist.
Take maintenance bronchodilators and inhaled corticosteroids strictly as scheduled.
Have a written COPD Exacerbation Action Plan detailing when to start emergency antibiotics or steroids.
warning_signs: Sudden, severe worsening of shortness of breath at rest
Change in sputum color (to dark green/brown), increased thickness, or blood in mucus
New or worsening confusion, extreme drowsiness, or morning headaches (signs of CO2 retention)
Swelling in ankles, legs, or feet (signs of cor pulmonale / right heart failure)
when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate emergency medical care for severe respiratory failure, blue lips, or confusion.
Contact your doctor promptly at the first sign of an acute flare-up or increased sputum production.
sources: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD)
World Health Organization (WHO) - COPD Fact Sheet

Malaria.description: Malaria is a life-threatening, preventable, and curable mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
symptoms: High fever, shaking chills, and profuse sweating (often in cyclical paroxysms)
Severe headaches and body/muscle aches
Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea
Abdominal pain and loss of appetite
Extreme fatigue and anemia
Jaundice (yellowish skin/eyes) in severe infections
risk_factors: Living in or traveling to tropical and subtropical malaria-endemic regions
Lack of mosquito protection (bed nets, repellent, indoor spraying)
Absence of prophylactic antimalarial medication during travel
Young children, pregnant women, and non-immune travelers (highest vulnerability)

prefer: Abundant fluids, clean water, oral rehydration salts (ORS), and coconut water
Fresh fruit juices, vegetable broths, and easy-to-digest soups
Soft carbohydrates (porridge, boiled rice, mashed potatoes)
Iron and protein rich foods (eggs, lentils) during recovery to rebuild red blood cells
limit: Oily, spicy, and deep-fried foods that provoke nausea and vomiting
Caffeinated beverages and alcohol
Heavy, hard-to-digest meals during the acute fever stage
food.general_tip: Maintain aggressive hydration with electrolyte-rich liquids and soft, easily digestible foods during the fever stage.

recommended: Complete bed rest throughout the acute infection and fever phases
No physical exertion until fully treated, fever-free, and hemoglobin levels recover
Gradual resumption of light daily walking after medical clearance
precautions: Strictly avoid any strenuous exercise or sports while infected (risk of splenic rupture if spleen is enlarged).
Rest adequately to allow bone marrow to regenerate red blood cells.

lifestyle: Sleep under insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs)
Apply DEET or picaridin-based insect repellents on exposed skin
Wear long-sleeved clothing and long pants during dusk and dawn
Take prescribed travel chemoprophylaxis when visiting endemic areas
monitoring: Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDTs) and microscopic blood smear examination (thick and thin films)
Complete blood counts to monitor hemoglobin, hematocrit, and platelet counts
Liver and renal function tests, blood glucose levels
medical_guidance: Seek immediate medical testing for any fever after traveling to a malaria-endemic area.
Complete the full prescribed course of Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT) or indicated antimalarials.
Never delay malaria treatment, as P. falciparum can progress to severe malaria within 24 hours.
warning_signs: Confusion, convulsions, coma, or altered consciousness (Cerebral Malaria)
Severe anemia, pale appearance, and extreme breathlessness (Acidosis)
Passing very dark or black urine ('Blackwater fever')
Persistent vomiting preventing oral medication intake
Sudden, severe drop in blood pressure and shock
when_to_seek_help: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency medical hospitalization for any sign of severe malaria, confusion, or dark urine.
Visit a clinic promptly for any unexplained fever following travel to tropical areas.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Malaria

Hepatitis_C.description: Hepatitis C is a viral infection caused by the Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) that causes liver inflammation, often leading to chronic infection, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.
common_types: Acute Hepatitis C (short-term, within first 6 months)
Chronic Hepatitis C (long-term, in >70-80% of untreated cases)
symptoms: Often asymptomatic for decades ('silent infection')
Chronic fatigue, malaise, and joint pain
Loss of appetite, nausea, and mild abdominal pain in upper right quadrant
Dark-colored urine and pale, clay-colored stools
Yellowing of skin and eyes (jaundice)
Easy bruising and bleeding
risk_factors: Sharing contaminated needles, syringes, or drug preparation equipment
Receiving blood transfusions or organ transplants before universal screening (e.g., before 1992)
Unregulated tattooing or body piercing with non-sterile equipment
Needlestick injuries in healthcare workers
Infants born to HCV-infected mothers

prefer: Fresh fruits and leafy green vegetables rich in antioxidants
Lean proteins (poultry, fish, legumes, tofu)
Whole grains (brown rice, oats, barley)
Moderate consumption of black, unsweetened coffee (shown in studies to support liver health)
limit: Alcohol (must be completely avoided; accelerates liver fibrosis and cirrhosis)
Raw or undercooked shellfish (risk of Vibrio vulnificus infection in liver disease)
High-fat, fried, and heavily processed foods
Excessive iron supplements unless specifically prescribed
food.general_tip: Follow a balanced, liver-protective Mediterranean-style diet and strictly eliminate all alcohol intake.

recommended: Moderate aerobic activities (walking, light cycling, swimming, 150 mins/week)
Light resistance and bodyweight exercises to maintain muscle mass
Stretching and yoga for stress reduction
precautions: Pace exercise sessions according to daily energy levels and liver status.
Avoid contact sports if spleen is enlarged or platelets are low.
Stay well hydrated during workouts.

lifestyle: Strictly abstain from all alcohol and recreational drugs
Get vaccinated against Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B to prevent dual viral infections
Avoid sharing personal hygiene items (razors, toothbrushes, nail clippers)
Review all over-the-counter medications and herbal supplements with your hepatologist
monitoring: HCV Antibody screening test followed by confirmatory HCV RNA PCR viral load
HCV Genotype testing
Liver Function Tests (ALT, AST, Bilirubin, Albumin, INR)
Non-invasive fibrosis assessment (FibroScan / transient elastography or APRI score)
Liver ultrasound screening every 6 months if cirrhosis is present
medical_guidance: Consult a hepatologist, gastroenterologist, or infectious disease specialist.
Complete a curative course of Direct-Acting Antiviral (DAA) therapy (typically 8 to 12 weeks with >95% cure rates).
Confirm cure with a Sustained Virologic Response test (SVR12) 12 weeks after completing DAA therapy.
warning_signs: Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry stools (Esophageal variceal bleeding)
Abdominal swelling with fluid accumulation (Ascites)
Confusion, disorientation, forgetfulness, or slurred speech (Hepatic Encephalopathy)
Rapid, progressive jaundice and dark urine
when_to_seek_help: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, or acute mental confusion.
Visit an infectious disease or liver clinic for curative DAA medication treatment.
sources: World Health Organization (WHO) - Hepatitis C Guidelines
American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) / IDSA HCV Guidance
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Hepatitis C

COVID_19.description: COVID-19 is a contagious respiratory and systemic illness caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which can range from mild upper respiratory symptoms to severe pneumonia, ARDS, and multi-organ failure.
common_types: Long COVID (Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 / PASC)
symptoms: Fever or chills
Cough (often dry, but can be productive)
Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Fatigue, muscle or body aches
New loss of taste or smell (anosmia/ageusia)
Sore throat, congestion, or runny nose
Nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea
risk_factors: Older age (65 years and older)
Underlying medical conditions (diabetes, chronic lung disease, heart disease, obesity, CKD)
Immunocompromised status
Unvaccinated status against COVID-19

prefer: Hydrating fluids (water, herbal teas, broths, electrolyte solutions)
Nutrient-dense fruits and vegetables rich in vitamins and zinc
Easily digestible proteins (eggs, soups, yogurt, tofu)
Small, frequent meals when appetite or smell is diminished
limit: Sugary sodas, energy drinks, and alcohol
Ultra-processed, salty snack foods
Heavily fried, greasy meals that worsen digestive upset
food.general_tip: Prioritize aggressive hydration, balanced protein intake, and antioxidant-rich foods to support immune response.

recommended: Complete rest during acute viral infection and fever
Gentle breathing exercises and proning (lying on stomach to improve oxygenation) if comfortable
Gradual, staged return to physical activity only after complete resolution of acute symptoms
precautions: Do not engage in aerobic or resistance workouts while febrile or short of breath.
Stop and rest immediately if post-exertional malaise, heart palpitations, or dizziness occur.
Follow medical guidance before resuming sports if you experienced cardiac symptoms.

lifestyle: Isolate from others to prevent viral transmission according to public health guidelines
Wear high-quality masks (N95/KN95) when around others
Ensure good indoor ventilation (open windows, HEPA filters)
Stay up to date with updated COVID-19 vaccines
monitoring: Home pulse oximetry monitoring (normal oxygen saturation is typically 95-100%)
Body temperature tracking
Rapid antigen or PCR diagnostic testing
Monitoring for lingering symptoms (Long COVID)
medical_guidance: Eligible high-risk patients should consult a doctor early regarding oral antivirals (e.g., Paxlovid) within 5 days of symptom onset.
Rest extensively and do not rush recovery.
Seek medical evaluation if symptoms rebound or fail to improve after 7-10 days.
warning_signs: Oxygen saturation dropping below 92-94% on room air
Trouble breathing, persistent pain or pressure in the chest
New confusion or inability to wake or stay awake
Pale, gray, or blue-colored skin, lips, or nail beds (cyanosis)
when_to_seek_help: Call emergency services IMMEDIATELY for severe shortness of breath, low oxygen levels, chest pressure, or cyanosis.
Contact your doctor promptly upon testing positive if you have high-risk chronic conditions.
sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - COVID-19 Guidelines
National Institutes of Health (NIH) - COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines

Liver_Disease.description: Liver disease encompasses various acute and chronic conditions that damage hepatic tissue, impairing liver metabolism, detoxification, bile production, and protein synthesis.
common_types: Viral Hepatitis (A, B, C, D, E)
symptoms: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes (jaundice)
Abdominal pain and swelling (especially in the right upper quadrant)
Chronic fatigue, weakness, and generalized malaise
Dark amber-colored urine and pale, clay-colored stools
Itchy skin (pruritus) without rash
Swelling in the legs, ankles, and abdomen (ascites)
Easy bruising and bleeding tendencies
risk_factors: Heavy and chronic alcohol consumption
Obesity, Type 2 diabetes, and high triglycerides (metabolic dysfunction)
Unprotected exposure to viral hepatitis
Overuse of hepatotoxic medications (e.g., chronic excessive acetaminophen) or unregulated herbal supplements
Exposure to industrial toxins and environmental chemicals

prefer: Fresh vegetables, cruciferous greens, and antioxidant-rich fruits
Moderate consumption of unsweetened black coffee (hepatoprotective properties)
Plant-based proteins (tofu, beans, lentils) and lean poultry/fish
Whole grains (oats, brown rice, quinoa)
Low-sodium home-prepared foods
limit: Alcohol in all forms (complete abstinence is essential in active liver disease)
High-sodium foods, canned items, and cured meats (worsens fluid retention/ascites)
Raw or undercooked shellfish and seafood
Excessive saturated fats, trans fats, and high-fructose corn syrup
food.general_tip: Adopt a low-sodium, nutrient-dense Mediterranean diet and strictly avoid all alcohol to reduce liver strain.

recommended: Regular moderate aerobic exercise (walking, stationary cycling, swimming, 150 mins/week)
Light resistance and strength training to prevent sarcopenia (muscle loss)
Gentle stretching and mobility routines
precautions: Avoid high-impact or contact sports if spleen is enlarged or if portal hypertension is present.
Exercise at a comfortable pace and avoid overexertion during fatigue flare-ups.
Ensure adequate hydration without exceeding fluid restrictions if prescribed.

lifestyle: Complete and permanent abstinence from alcohol
Maintain a healthy body weight and waist circumference
Get vaccinated against Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B
Review all prescription drugs, OTC pain relievers, and supplements with a hepatologist
monitoring: Liver Function Tests (ALT, AST, Alkaline Phosphatase, Total Bilirubin, Albumin, INR)
Abdominal ultrasound, FibroScan (transient elastography), or MRI
Alpha-Fetoprotein (AFP) blood tests and 6-monthly ultrasounds for liver cancer surveillance in cirrhosis
Platelet counts and complete blood counts
medical_guidance: Work collaboratively with a hepatologist or gastroenterologist.
Identify and treat the specific underlying cause (e.g., antiviral therapy, weight reduction, alcohol cessation).
Never take high doses of acetaminophen or untested dietary supplements.
warning_signs: Vomiting blood or passing black, tarry, foul-smelling stools (gastrointestinal hemorrhage)
Sudden, severe confusion, disorientation, lethargy, or hand tremors (Hepatic Encephalopathy)
Rapidly expanding, tense abdominal swelling with fever and abdominal tenderness (Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis)
Deep jaundice with severe generalized itching
when_to_seek_help: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, acute confusion, or fever with abdominal swelling.
Consult a physician promptly for new onset jaundice, dark urine, or unexplained persistent fatigue.
sources: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL)

Maternal_Health_Risk.description: Maternal health risk refers to conditions, complications, and high-risk factors that affect maternal and fetal well-being during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period.
symptoms: Severe, persistent headaches or vision changes (flashing lights, blurring)
Sudden swelling (edema) of face, hands, or feet
High blood pressure readings (>140/90 mmHg)
Severe upper right abdominal pain (under the ribs)
Vaginal bleeding or fluid leakage during pregnancy
Noticeable decrease or cessation in fetal movements
Persistent severe nausea and vomiting with inability to keep liquids down
risk_factors: Maternal age (under 18 or over 35 years)
Pre-existing chronic conditions (hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, autoimmune disorders)
History of preeclampsia or gestational diabetes in a prior pregnancy
Multiple gestation (twins, triplets)
Obesity, severe anemia, or malnutrition
Lack of regular prenatal medical care

prefer: Nutrient-dense, balanced meals with adequate lean protein, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats
Folate/folic acid-rich foods and prenatal vitamins
Iron-rich foods (spinach, lentils, lean meats) combined with Vitamin C
Calcium and Vitamin D rich foods (pasteurized dairy, fortified plant milk)
Abundant clean drinking water and fluids
limit: Raw or undercooked meats, poultry, sushi, and runny eggs (Listeria/Toxoplasma risk)
Unpasteurized dairy products, soft cheeses, and unpasteurized juices
High-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel, tilefish)
Alcohol and tobacco (must be strictly avoided)
Excessive caffeine (keep below 200 mg/day as recommended)
food.general_tip: Follow a balanced, well-cooked prenatal diet rich in iron, calcium, and folate, accompanied by prescribed prenatal vitamins.

recommended: Prenatal walking on level, secure surfaces (30 mins most days)
Prenatal swimming, water aerobics, and stationary cycling
Prenatal yoga, pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, and gentle stretching
precautions: Avoid contact sports, hot yoga, and activities with falling or abdominal impact risks.
Avoid lying flat on your back (supine position) after the first trimester.
Stop immediately and seek care if experiencing vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, dizziness, or contractions.

lifestyle: Attend all scheduled prenatal and postpartum medical visits
Strictly avoid alcohol, tobacco, vaping, and non-prescribed medications
Get adequate rest and sleep on your side (preferably left side) to optimize placental blood flow
Monitor blood pressure and fetal movements as advised by your obstetrician
monitoring: Regular prenatal blood pressure, weight, and urine protein checks at every visit
Routine blood tests (CBC, blood type/Rh antibody screen, rubella, infectious disease panel)
Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) for gestational diabetes screening at 24-28 weeks
Obstetric ultrasounds for fetal growth, anatomy, and placental evaluation
Daily fetal kick counts in the third trimester
medical_guidance: Maintain close communication with your obstetrician, certified nurse-midwife, or maternal-fetal medicine specialist.
Never take over-the-counter medications, herbal teas, or supplements without obstetric clearance.
Attend postpartum checkups to monitor blood pressure, healing, and mental health.
warning_signs: Sudden, severe headache not relieved by acetaminophen, accompanied by blurred vision or spots
Vaginal bleeding or sudden gush of clear fluid (water breaking prematurely)
Sudden significant decrease in baby's movements
Severe, sharp pain in upper right abdomen or severe continuous pelvic pain
Fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher with chills
when_to_seek_help: Go to the nearest Labor & Delivery triage / emergency hospital IMMEDIATELY for vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, decreased fetal movements, or severe headaches with visual disturbances.
Contact your obstetric team promptly for any concerning symptoms or blood pressure >140/90 mmHg.
sources: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
World Health Organization (WHO) - Maternal and Perinatal Health
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Hear Her Campaign

Dermatological_Diseases.description: Dermatological diseases comprise a broad range of inflammatory, allergic, infectious, and autoimmune conditions that affect the skin, hair, nails, and mucous membranes.
symptoms: Redness, inflammation, and erythema on the skin
Intense itching (pruritus), burning, or stinging sensation
Dry, cracked, scaly, or flaking skin patches
Raised bumps, blisters, pustules, or hives
Thickened, leathery skin plaques with silvery scales (in psoriasis)
Skin oozing, crusting, or weeping
risk_factors: Genetic predisposition and family history of eczema, psoriasis, or allergies
Immune system dysregulation or autoimmune tendencies
Environmental allergens, harsh soaps, detergents, and fragrances
Extreme weather, dry air, and temperature fluctuations
Psychological stress, sleep deprivation, and friction

prefer: Anti-inflammatory foods (berries, leafy greens, wild salmon, walnuts)
Foods rich in Omega-3 fatty acids and Vitamin E (avocados, seeds, olive oil)
Zinc-rich foods (beans, pumpkin seeds, whole grains) to support skin repair
Abundant water and hydrating herbal teas
limit: Ultra-processed foods, high-sugar snacks, and artificial additives
Excessive dairy, refined carbohydrates, and saturated fats (which can trigger acne flare-ups in some individuals)
Alcohol and excessive spicy foods (common triggers for rosacea and flushing)
food.general_tip: Consume an anti-inflammatory, antioxidant-rich diet and stay well hydrated to support skin barrier integrity.

recommended: Moderate cardiovascular exercises in temperature-controlled indoor spaces
Swimming in clean, well-maintained pools (rinse and moisturize immediately afterward)
Yoga, stretching, and low-impact resistance training
precautions: Wear loose-fitting, breathable, 100% cotton exercise clothing to minimize friction.
Shower promptly after sweating with lukewarm water and a gentle, soap-free cleanser.
Apply hypoallergenic moisturizer within 3 minutes of patting skin dry (soak and seal method).

lifestyle: Take short (5-10 minute), lukewarm showers; avoid hot water which strips skin oils
Use fragrance-free, dye-free cleansers, laundry detergents, and moisturizers
Keep fingernails trimmed short to minimize skin damage and infection from scratching
Use an indoor humidifier during dry winter months
monitoring: Regular monitoring of skin lesions, plaque coverage, and flare-up frequency
Tracking individual trigger exposures (foods, personal care products, weather, stress)
Periodic skin checks by a board-certified dermatologist
medical_guidance: Consult a dermatologist for accurate diagnostic evaluation and specialized treatment.
Use topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, biologics, or systemic treatments strictly as directed.
Do not apply harsh over-the-counter astringents, alcohol rubs, or unverified home remedies to inflamed skin.
warning_signs: Rapidly spreading redness, extreme heat, swelling, and severe pain (Cellulitis / Bacterial infection)
Widespread blistering, skin peeling, and high fever (Medical emergencies like SJS/TEN or Erythrodermic Psoriasis)
Facial swelling, lip/tongue swelling, and breathing difficulty accompanying hives (Anaphylaxis)
Yellow pus-filled crusts with increasing warmth (Staphylococcal superinfection)
when_to_seek_help: Seek IMMEDIATE emergency care for hives accompanied by breathing difficulty or throat swelling (Anaphylaxis), or rapid skin detachment.
Consult a dermatologist promptly for non-healing rashes, severe pain, spreading infection, or unmanageable itching.
